topic: Solar system; stability of orbital motions; satellites (physics only)
subject: physics

items.q: Which list correctly describes what our solar system contains?
items.correct: One star, the eight planets, the dwarf planets and the planets' moons
items.misconception: One star and the eight planets that orbit around it, nothing else
items.why: Primary-school posters show a Sun and eight planets in a row, so anything missing from that picture is not counted as a member. The specification lists the members as one star, the eight planets, the dwarf planets, and the natural satellites that orbit planets. All of them belong.
items.random_wrong: One star, nine planets including Pluto, and the moons of those

items.q: What is meant by a natural satellite?
items.correct: A moon: a body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun
items.misconception: A small rocky body that orbits the Sun directly, between the planets
items.why: Students learn that everything in the solar system 'goes round the Sun' and apply that to moons as well. Moons orbit planets; the planets in turn orbit the Sun. That is why moons are called natural satellites of their planet.
items.random_wrong: A dwarf planet, which orbits the Sun beyond the eight planets

items.q: Which statement describes how our solar system relates to the Milky Way?
items.correct: Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
items.misconception: The Milky Way is just another name for our own solar system
items.why: Both words describe 'everything out there' in casual use, so the scale difference between them is never registered. A galaxy is a huge collection of many billions of stars. The Milky Way contains our solar system, not the other way round.
items.random_wrong: The Milky Way galaxy holds everything in the universe

items.q: How was the Sun formed?
items.correct: From a cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity
items.misconception: From a cloud of dust and gas squeezed together by magnetism
items.why: Magnetism is the attraction students meet most often in the lab, and 'squeezing' feels more active than a pull. The specification states that the Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.
items.random_wrong: From a huge ball of chemical fuel that was set alight in space

items.q: At the start of a star's life cycle, why do fusion reactions begin?
items.correct: Gravity draws the dust and gas together, heating it until nuclei fuse
items.misconception: The dust and gas catch fire and burn chemically, giving out the energy
items.why: The everyday word 'burning' is used for the Sun, which suggests a chemical reaction with a fuel. No chemical burning takes place. Gravitational collapse raises the temperature and density until nuclei fuse.
items.random_wrong: Fusion starts as soon as gravity begins to draw the cloud inwards

items.q: Which two effects are in equilibrium in a stable star?
items.correct: The gravitational collapse inwards and the expansion due to fusion energy
items.misconception: No effects at all, because equilibrium means no forces act on it
items.why: 'Balanced' is heard as 'nothing happening', so students picture a star with the forces switched off. Equilibrium means the inward and outward effects are equal and opposite, so the star stays the same size. Both are still acting.
items.random_wrong: The inward pull of gravity and the outward push of gravity itself

items.q: A main sequence star stays the same size for billions of years. Why?
items.correct: Its inward collapse and its outward expansion stay balanced
items.misconception: No forces act inside a star once it reaches the main sequence
items.why: 'Balanced' is heard as 'nothing happening', so students picture a star with the forces switched off. Equilibrium means the inward and outward effects are equal and opposite, so the star stays the same size. Both are still acting.
items.random_wrong: Gravity pushes the star outwards as hard as it pulls it inwards

items.q: What determines the life cycle that a star will follow?
items.correct: The size of the star, which sets the path it takes
items.misconception: The colour of the star, which shows its surface state
items.why: Colour is the most visible property of a star, so it is assumed to be the property that matters. The specification states that the life cycle is determined by the size of the star. Mass decides which path a star takes.
items.random_wrong: How bright the star looks when viewed from Earth

items.q: A star about the size of the Sun leaves the main sequence. What happens next?
items.correct: It expands and becomes a red giant
items.misconception: It explodes straight away as a supernova
items.why: The supernova is the dramatic ending everyone remembers, so it gets applied to every star. Only stars much more massive than the Sun explode as supernovae. A Sun-sized star ends as a white dwarf.
items.random_wrong: It shrinks back to become a protostar

items.q: What is the full sequence of stages at the end of the life of a star about the size of the Sun?
items.correct: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf
items.misconception: Red giant, then supernova, then a neutron star
items.why: The supernova is the dramatic ending everyone remembers, so it gets applied to every star. Only stars much more massive than the Sun explode as supernovae. A Sun-sized star ends as a white dwarf.
items.random_wrong: Red super giant, then supernova, then black hole

items.q: What happens to a star much more massive than the Sun after the main sequence?
items.correct: Red super giant, then supernova, then neutron star or black hole
items.misconception: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf, just as the Sun will
items.why: Colour is the most visible property of a star, so it is assumed to be the property that matters. The specification states that the life cycle is determined by the size of the star. Mass decides which path a star takes.
items.random_wrong: Red super giant, then supernova, then always a black hole

items.q: What can be left at the centre after a massive star explodes as a supernova?
items.correct: A neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough
items.misconception: A black hole, whatever the mass of the star that exploded
items.why: Black holes are the best-known object linked to dying massive stars, so they are assumed to be the only outcome. A supernova leaves a neutron star; only the most massive stars leave a black hole.
items.random_wrong: A white dwarf that later cools to become a black dwarf

items.q: Which elements are produced by fusion processes in stars?
items.correct: All of the naturally occurring elements
items.misconception: Only hydrogen and helium, and nothing more
items.why: Fusion is usually introduced with hydrogen forming helium, and students stop the story there. Fusion in stars builds heavier and heavier nuclei, producing all the naturally occurring elements between them.
items.random_wrong: Only those elements that are heavier than iron

items.q: Where are the elements heavier than iron produced?
items.correct: In the explosion of a massive star, a supernova
items.misconception: In the fusion reactions inside a main sequence star
items.why: If fusion makes elements, it seems natural that it makes all of them in the same place. The specification is specific: elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova, not in normal stellar fusion.
items.random_wrong: Nowhere; they have existed from the very start

items.q: What does the explosion of a massive star do to the elements it has produced?
items.correct: It distributes the elements throughout the whole universe
items.misconception: It leaves the elements locked inside the remnant star
items.why: The remnant is described as what is 'left behind', which suggests everything else stayed put too. The supernova explosion throws the star's material outwards, spreading the elements through the universe.
items.random_wrong: It destroys the elements, leaving only hydrogen gas

items.q: How do fusion processes in stars lead to the formation of new elements?
items.correct: Small nuclei join to form larger nuclei of different elements
items.misconception: Large nuclei split apart to form smaller nuclei of new elements
items.why: Fusion and fission are taught close together and are easily swapped. Fusion joins nuclei; fission splits them. New, heavier elements form in stars because nuclei fuse.
items.random_wrong: Atoms join chemically to make new compounds and elements

items.q: What allows a planet or a satellite to maintain a circular orbit?
items.correct: Gravity provides the force that keeps it in its circular orbit
items.misconception: There is no gravity in space, so it just keeps drifting round
items.why: Astronauts are seen floating, which is taken as proof that gravity has run out. Gravity acts over vast distances and is exactly what holds a body in orbit. Without it the body would travel in a straight line.
items.random_wrong: Its engines fire all the time to hold it in its orbital path

items.q: Which statement correctly compares moons and artificial satellites?
items.correct: Both orbit a planet; moons are natural and satellites are man-made
items.misconception: Both orbit a planet, but only the moon is held there by gravity
items.why: Rockets need engines to launch, so students assume the engines must keep running to stay up there. Once in orbit a satellite needs no engine. Gravity supplies the force for the circular orbit, exactly as it does for a moon.
items.random_wrong: Both orbit the Sun directly, and both were formed with the Sun

items.q: (HT only) A satellite travels round a circular orbit at a steady rate. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Its speed stays the same but its velocity is changing
items.misconception: Its speed and its velocity are both remaining constant
items.why: In everyday language speed and velocity mean the same thing, so a constant rate seems to fix both. Velocity is speed in a given direction. In a circular orbit the direction changes continuously, so the velocity changes even though the speed does not.
items.random_wrong: Its speed keeps increasing because gravity acts upon it

items.q: (HT only) A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel faster. For the orbit to stay stable, what must happen?
items.correct: The radius of the orbit must get smaller
items.misconception: The radius of the orbit must become much larger
items.why: Whirling an object on a string, or a fairground ride, suggests that going faster throws you outwards. For a stable orbit, a greater speed means a smaller radius and a smaller speed means a larger radius.
items.random_wrong: The radius of the orbit can stay exactly as before

items.q: Is the Sun a planet or a star?
items.correct: The Sun is a star, and it is the only star in our solar system.
items.misconception: The Sun is just a very large, very hot planet at the centre.
items.why: The Sun is drawn in the same diagram as the planets and looks like one more circle, and students rarely see it grouped with other stars. A star releases energy by fusion reactions in its core; a planet does not. The Sun is the one star of the solar system.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many planets orbit the Sun?
items.correct: Eight. Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets.
items.misconception: Nine, because Pluto is still one of the planets.
items.why: Older books, songs and mnemonics learned before 2006 still list nine planets. The specification states that the solar system has eight planets plus dwarf planets. Pluto is one of the dwarf planets.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the Milky Way the whole universe?
items.correct: No. The Milky Way is one galaxy among a great many in the universe.
items.misconception: The Milky Way galaxy is the entire universe.
items.why: The Milky Way is the only galaxy most students can name, so it becomes a stand-in for everything. The universe contains billions of galaxies. The Milky Way is simply the one that our solar system sits in.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does fusion begin as soon as a cloud starts to collapse?
items.correct: No. Gravity must first compress and heat the material until it is hot and dense enough for fusion.
items.misconception: Fusion starts the moment gravity begins drawing the dust and gas together.
items.why: The life cycle is taught as a list of stages, so the gap between 'gravity pulls' and 'fusion starts' is easy to miss. Fusion needs extreme temperature and pressure. These are produced by the gravitational collapse, so collapse comes first.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What balances gravity in a main sequence star?
items.correct: The expansion caused by the energy released in fusion reactions balances the gravitational collapse.
items.misconception: Gravity itself pushes outwards as well as pulling inwards, so it balances itself.
items.why: Students know gravity is the only named force in the topic, so they make it do both jobs. Gravity acts inwards only. The outward effect comes from the energy released by fusion in the core.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the red giant stage come in the life cycle?
items.correct: After the main sequence stage, when the star leaves the main sequence.
items.misconception: Before the main sequence, because a young star must be large first.
items.why: Students associate 'giant' with the early growth of the star from a big cloud rather than with its old age. The order is protostar, then main sequence star, then red giant. The giant stage belongs to the end of the star's life.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which is larger, a red giant or a white dwarf?
items.correct: The red giant is far larger; the white dwarf is the small dense remnant left when it collapses.
items.misconception: The white dwarf is a large bright star that forms before the red giant stage.
items.why: The word 'white' suggests hot and bright, which students equate with big and young. A white dwarf is very small and very dense. It is the late-stage remnant of a Sun-sized star, formed after the red giant stage.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does a supernova do to the elements a star has made?
items.correct: The explosion distributes the elements throughout the universe.
items.misconception: The explosion destroys the elements, breaking them back down into hydrogen.
items.why: 'Explosion' is read as total destruction, so the material is assumed to be lost rather than scattered. The supernova throws the material outwards, spreading the elements through the universe where they can form new stars and planets.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In which direction does gravity act on a satellite in a circular orbit?
items.correct: Towards the centre of the orbit, at right angles to the direction the satellite is moving.
items.misconception: Along the direction of travel, so it makes the satellite go faster and faster.
items.why: Students expect a force to speed things up, because that is what a force does in straight-line motion. The gravitational force is perpendicular to the motion in a circular orbit, so it changes the direction only, not the speed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an orbiting body change speed and keep the same radius?
items.correct: No. For a stable orbit at a given radius there is only one possible speed, so the radius must change if the speed changes.
items.misconception: Yes, a satellite can orbit at any speed it likes at a fixed radius.
items.why: Cars can be driven round the same roundabout at different speeds, and that everyday picture is carried over to orbits. A stable orbit requires gravity to match the circular motion exactly, so each radius allows only one orbital speed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where is our solar system in the Milky Way?
items.correct: It lies in one of the spiral arms, far out from the centre of the galaxy.
items.misconception: Our solar system sits at the centre of the Milky Way galaxy.
items.why: Diagrams put the Sun at the middle of the page, and the Sun is already the centre of the solar system. The Milky Way contains many billions of stars. Our solar system is a small part of it, well away from the centre.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What holds a star up against its own gravity?
items.correct: The expansion caused by the energy released in fusion reactions.
items.misconception: An upthrust from the gas surrounding the star, as with a floating object.
items.why: Upthrust is the balancing force students meet in the forces topic, so it is reused here. There is no surrounding fluid to provide upthrust. The outward effect comes from the fusion energy released in the core.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does how bright a star looks from Earth decide its life cycle?
items.correct: No. The life cycle is determined by the size of the star.
items.misconception: The brighter a star looks from Earth, the longer and more dramatic its life cycle.
items.why: Brightness in the sky is the only stellar measurement students make themselves, so it feels important. Apparent brightness depends mostly on distance. It is the size, or mass, of a star that determines its life cycle.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all stars eventually become supergiants if they live long enough?
items.correct: No. Only stars much more massive than the Sun become red super giants.
items.misconception: Every star becomes a supergiant in the end; it is just a matter of age.
items.why: The life cycle is presented as a single chart, so students read it as one path everything travels along. There are two paths, and which one a star takes is fixed by its size. Age moves a star along its own path only.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an orbiting body held in place by an outward force?
items.correct: No. Gravity is the only force needed; it acts towards the centre of the orbit.
items.misconception: An outward force balances gravity and holds the body at a fixed distance.
items.why: Being thrown outwards on a roundabout feels like an outward force, so it is assumed to exist in orbit too. The felt outward push is an effect of the body's own motion, not a force acting on it. Gravity alone maintains the orbit.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which is constant in a circular orbit, the speed or the velocity?
items.correct: The speed is constant; the velocity changes because the direction changes.
items.misconception: The velocity is constant and it is the speed that keeps changing.
items.why: The two words are learned as a pair and their definitions are easily swapped over under pressure. Velocity includes direction, so it is the quantity that changes on a curved path. The speed stays the same.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
